Sherlock

A neural network
with nothing hidden

Sherlock reads handwritten digits. It has no framework underneath it — no PyTorch, no TensorFlow, just NumPy and about 200 lines of Python. That makes it small enough to open up completely. Every formula on this page is a line of code in the repository, and every number is measured from the trained model, not illustrated.

Michal Pospíšil · Matouš Rubek · Štěpán Dupač
784→128→10 multilayer perceptron · trained on MNIST · github: Sherlock-Model

Live forward pass
Every bar, every square and every number updates on each stroke. The 128 middle squares are the hidden layer — bright means that feature detector fired.
Stage 1 — the input

A picture is just 784 numbers in a row

The network never sees a picture. It sees a vector: the 28×28 grid of pixels read left-to-right, top-to-bottom, flattened into a single row of 784 values. Each value is a brightness scaled to the range 0 (paper) to 1 (ink).

That flattening throws away something real — the network is not told that pixel 100 sits directly above pixel 128. It has to rediscover that relationship from the data. Hover the grid below to see which entry of the vector each pixel becomes.

a single training example
\[ \mathbf{x} \;=\; \big[x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_{784}\big] \in [0,1]^{784}, \qquad x_j \;=\; \frac{\text{pixel}_j}{255} \]
Pixel ↔ vector indexhover a pixel
Row-major order, the same order reshape(-1, 784) produces in mnist.py. Ink concentrates in the middle: the border pixels are almost always 0, which is why the model can afford to ignore them.
Stage 2 — preprocessing

Making your handwriting look like MNIST

MNIST digits are not raw scans. Every one of them was size-normalised and centred by its centre of mass before the dataset was published. A model trained on that convention only works on images that follow it — so preprocess.py has to reproduce the convention exactly for anything you draw or upload.

Step through the eight stages below on four real inputs. Two are MNIST digits; two are images drawn from scratch as black ink on a white page, which is the opposite polarity and forces the auto-inversion to trigger.

The pipeline, stage by stage

Why centring is not optional

The last stage shifts the image so its centre of mass lands on the middle pixel. Removing just that one stage — everything else identical — gives the network a different picture of the same digit, and it is a picture unlike anything in its training set.

Ablation: the same image, with the centring step disabled
Both versions are run through the real trained network. The confidence difference is the cost of skipping one stage.
Stage 3 — the forward pass

Two matrix multiplications, and that is the entire model

Sherlock has two layers. The first turns 784 pixels into 128 features; the second turns those 128 features into 10 scores, one per digit. Between them sits a non-linearity. That is genuinely all of it.

layer 1 — 784 pixels become 128 features
\[ \mathbf{z}^{(1)} = \mathbf{x} W^{(1)} + \mathbf{b}^{(1)}, \qquad \mathbf{a}^{(1)} = \mathrm{ReLU}\!\left(\mathbf{z}^{(1)}\right) \]
layer 2 — 128 features become 10 scores
\[ \mathbf{z}^{(2)} = \mathbf{a}^{(1)} W^{(2)} + \mathbf{b}^{(2)}, \qquad \mathbf{p} = \mathrm{softmax}\!\left(\mathbf{z}^{(2)}\right) \]
W(1)
784 × 128 weight matrix — 100,352 numbers
b(1)
128 biases, one per hidden unit
W(2)
128 × 10 weight matrix — 1,280 numbers
b(2)
10 biases, one per digit
z(2)
the logits — raw scores, before they become probabilities

Adding those up: 100,352 + 128 + 1,280 + 10 = 101,770 parameters. Every one of them starts as a random number and is nudged 25,800 times during training.

What one hidden unit actually computes

A single hidden unit is a weighted sum over all 784 pixels. Its weights can be folded back into a 28×28 image — a template that the unit is looking for. Orange means "ink here raises my output", blue means "ink here lowers it".

hidden unit i, written out in full
\[ z^{(1)}_i \;=\; \sum_{j=1}^{784} x_j\,W^{(1)}_{j,i} \;+\; b^{(1)}_i \]
Hidden unit inspector
Click any of the 128 tiles. The large panel shows that unit's template, and the bar shows what it currently outputs for the digit you drew in the live demo above.
src/model.py — the entire forward passdef forward(params, X):
    cache = [X]
    A = X
    last = len(params) - 1
    for i, (W, b) in enumerate(params):
        Z = A @ W + b                                  # the matrix multiply
        A = softmax(Z) if i == last else np.maximum(Z, 0.0)   # ReLU, or softmax at the end
        cache += [Z, A]                                # kept for the backward pass
    return A, cache
Stage 4 — the non-linearity

ReLU: the simplest possible way to bend a straight line

Stack two matrix multiplications with nothing between them and you get… one matrix multiplication. (xA)B = x(AB). The whole network would collapse into a single linear map, and a linear map cannot separate digits. Something non-linear has to sit in the middle.

ReLU is the least complicated choice that works: keep positives, zero out negatives.

rectified linear unit, and its derivative
\[ \mathrm{ReLU}(z) = \max(0, z) \qquad\qquad \frac{d}{dz}\mathrm{ReLU}(z) = \begin{cases} 1 & z > 0 \\ 0 & z \le 0 \end{cases} \]
The function
A hinge at the origin. That single kink is what lets stacked layers express curved decision boundaries.
How often each unit fires

The gradient is a gate

Because the derivative is either 1 or 0, ReLU acts as a switch during learning. Units that were silent for an example receive no gradient from it at all — the error signal simply stops there. This is the (cache[2*i-1] > 0) mask in the backward pass, and it is why a unit that goes permanently silent can never recover. That failure mode is called a dead unit.

Stage 5 — scores to probabilities, and a number to minimise

Softmax turns 10 scores into 10 probabilities

The last layer emits ten unbounded real numbers. To compare them against a true answer we need them to be positive and to sum to 1. Softmax exponentiates each score and normalises.

softmax over the 10 logits
\[ p_k \;=\; \frac{e^{z_k}}{\sum_{m=1}^{10} e^{z_m}} \qquad \text{so that } p_k > 0 \text{ and } \sum_k p_k = 1 \]
Softmax, hands ondrag the logits
Softmax cares only about differences between logits. Add the same constant to all ten and the probabilities do not move — which is exactly the trick the code uses to stay numerically safe.

The overflow trap, and how the code avoids it

\(e^{z}\) overflows a 64-bit float once \(z\) passes about 710. Since shifting all logits by a constant leaves the result unchanged, the code subtracts the row maximum first. The largest exponent then becomes \(e^0 = 1\), and overflow is impossible.

the shift-invariance that makes it safe
\[ \frac{e^{z_k - c}}{\sum_m e^{z_m - c}} = \frac{e^{-c}\,e^{z_k}}{e^{-c}\sum_m e^{z_m}} = \frac{e^{z_k}}{\sum_m e^{z_m}} \qquad \text{for any } c \] 
src/model.pydef softmax(Z):
    Z = Z - Z.max(axis=1, keepdims=True)     # c = row max, so the largest exponent is e^0
    E = np.exp(Z)
    return E / E.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)

Cross-entropy: how wrong is this guess?

The loss looks at one number only — the probability the model assigned to the correct digit — and takes its negative logarithm. Assign 1.0 to the truth and the loss is 0. Assign something near 0 and the loss climbs without bound.

cross-entropy for one example with true label y
\[ L \;=\; -\log p_y \]
averaged over a mini-batch of B examples
\[ \mathcal{L} \;=\; -\frac{1}{B}\sum_{n=1}^{B} \log p^{(n)}_{y_n} \]
Why the logarithm
The curve is gentle when the model is roughly right and brutal when it is confidently wrong. That asymmetry is what pushes the model to stop making overconfident mistakes.

A model that has learned nothing spreads its probability evenly, giving \(p_y = 0.1\) and a loss of \(-\log 0.1 \approx 2.303\). That value is the baseline to beat — and you will see it again in the failed training runs further down.

Everything above and below is easier to trust once you have watched it happen on numbers you can verify yourself. Here is a 3→2→2 network with a batch of two examples, following the identical conventions as the real code: row-vector batches, Z = A @ W + b, ReLU, softmax, mean cross-entropy.

Step through all 25 stages. Every matrix was computed by running the real functions.

One gradient step, in 25 stages
Stage 7 — backpropagation

Assigning blame to 101,770 numbers at once

The loss is one number. To improve it we need to know, for every single weight, whether nudging it up would raise or lower that number — the partial derivative \(\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial W\). Computing those one at a time would require 101,770 separate forward passes per step.

Backpropagation gets all of them in one backward sweep, by applying the chain rule from the loss backwards through the layers and reusing every intermediate result.

The gradient at the output is remarkably clean

Softmax and cross-entropy are messy on their own. Composed, almost everything cancels and the gradient at the logits becomes just prediction minus truth:

the starting point of the backward pass
\[ \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{z}^{(2)}} \;=\; \frac{\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{y}}{B} \]
If the model says 0.7 for a digit that is correct, that coordinate carries \(-0.3\): push it up. If it says 0.7 for a digit that is wrong, it carries \(+0.7\): push it down, hard. The B keeps the step size independent of batch size.

Then the same two moves, repeated per layer

gradients for a layer, given the gradient at its output
\[ \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial W^{(\ell)}} = \left(\mathbf{a}^{(\ell-1)}\right)^{\!\top} \delta^{(\ell)}, \qquad \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{b}^{(\ell)}} = \sum_{n} \delta^{(\ell)}_n \]
and the signal handed to the layer below
\[ \delta^{(\ell-1)} \;=\; \underbrace{\left(\delta^{(\ell)} \big(W^{(\ell)}\big)^{\!\top}\right)}_{\text{propagate}} \;\odot\; \underbrace{\mathbb{1}\!\left[\mathbf{z}^{(\ell-1)} > 0\right]}_{\text{ReLU gate}} \] 
src/model.py — those formulas, verbatimdef backward(params, cache, Y):
    L, B = len(params), Y.shape[0]
    grads = [None] * L
    dZ = (cache[2 * L] - Y) / B                     # (p - y) / B
    for i in range(L - 1, -1, -1):
        A_prev = cache[2 * i]
        grads[i] = [A_prev.T @ dZ, dZ.sum(axis=0)]   # dW and db
        if i > 0:
            dA = dZ @ params[i][0].T                  # propagate back
            dZ = dA * (cache[2 * i - 1] > 0)         # ReLU gate
    return grads

One weight, traced end to end

Here is the chain rule expanded for a single weight in the micro-network — every factor, every path, and the product that has to equal the gradient the code produced.

Chain rule for a single weight

Proving the derivation is right

A wrong gradient does not crash — it just trains badly, which is nearly impossible to debug by staring at loss curves. So gradcheck.py checks the calculus numerically: nudge one weight by \(\pm\varepsilon\), measure how the loss actually moved, and compare against what backprop claimed.

central difference versus the analytic gradient
\[ \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial w} \;\approx\; \frac{\mathcal{L}(w + \varepsilon) - \mathcal{L}(w - \varepsilon)}{2\varepsilon}, \qquad \text{relative error} = \frac{\left|\text{numeric} - \text{analytic}\right|} {\left|\text{numeric}\right| + \left|\text{analytic}\right|} \]
Gradient check — the real run, before training started
Anything below 1e-7 is float64 rounding noise rather than a mistake in the derivation. train.py asserts this before every training run, so training cannot start on broken calculus.
Stage 8 — gradient descent

Walking downhill in 101,770 dimensions

The gradient points in the direction of steepest increase. To reduce the loss, step the other way. The size of that step is the learning rate, and it is the single most consequential number in the whole project.

the update rule — this is the entire optimiser
\[ W \;\leftarrow\; W \;-\; \eta\,\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial W}, \qquad \mathbf{b} \;\leftarrow\; \mathbf{b} \;-\; \eta\,\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{b}} \]
η
the learning rate — 0.1 in this project

Roll a ball down a surface

Before the real thing, the idea in two dimensions. Pick a starting point and a learning rate, and watch the steps. Too small and it crawls; too large and it overshoots the valley and climbs the opposite wall.

Gradient descent playground
Click anywhere on the surface to drop the ball there. The arrows are the actual steps taken by the update rule above, on the surface shown.

The same question, on the real loss

Now the genuine article. Starting from Sherlock's real initial weights, we compute the real gradient and walk along it, measuring the true loss at each distance. This is a one-dimensional slice through 101,770-dimensional space, along the exact direction the first training step took.

Loss along the true gradient direction

Stochastic: why the model never sees the whole dataset at once

Computing the gradient on all 55,000 images gives the most accurate direction, but it buys one step. Instead the code takes a random mini-batch of 64, gets a noisy estimate of the gradient, and steps immediately — 860 times per epoch instead of once.

The noise is visible and it is not a defect. Individual batches disagree, so the loss zig-zags downward rather than descending smoothly, and that jitter helps the optimiser escape shallow traps.

Every single update of the first three epochs 2,580 mini-batches, real values
Faint line: the loss on each individual batch. Solid line: a 40-step running mean. The spread between them is the stochasticity.

The path the run actually took

Finally, the real loss surface. We take the 31 weight-vector snapshots saved during training, find the 2D plane that best contains that trajectory, and evaluate the true loss across it. This plane captures of the run's total movement — so this is close to the real shape of the descent, not an analogy.

Loss landscape and the path of the real training run hover the surface
Stage 9 — the training run

Thirty epochs, and knowing when to stop

An epoch is one pass over the training set. The data is reshuffled each time so the model never sees the same batch composition twice. After each epoch the code measures the loss on both the training set and a held-out validation set of 5,000 images the model never learns from.

The gap between those two curves is the story of the whole run.

Loss and accuracy across 30 epochs

Overfitting, and the answer to it

Training loss keeps falling essentially to zero — the model is memorising. Validation loss falls, flattens, and then drifts upward: the model is getting better at the training set and no better at the world. model.py handles this by keeping a copy of the weights from whichever epoch had the lowest validation loss, and returning those instead of the final ones. That is early stopping.

src/model.py — five lines that prevent overfitting from matteringtr_loss, tr_acc = evaluate(params, Xtr, ytr)
va_loss, va_acc = evaluate(params, Xva, yva)
history.append((epoch, tr_loss, va_loss, tr_acc, va_acc))
if va_loss < best[0]:                  # early stopping: keep the best
    best = (va_loss, [[W.copy(), b.copy()] for W, b in params])

Reporting the result honestly

The test set is touched exactly once, at the very end. Because it is a finite sample, the accuracy has genuine uncertainty, and train.py reports a 95% confidence interval rather than a bare number:

95% confidence interval for a proportion
\[ \hat{a} \;\pm\; 1.96\sqrt{\frac{\hat{a}\,(1-\hat{a})}{n}} \]
Quoting the interval keeps the comparison fair: a rival model at 98.0% is not meaningfully better than this one, because the intervals overlap.
Stage 10 — the knobs

What happens when you turn each dial

Learning rateη from 0.001 to 3.0
Initialisation — and why zeros destroy the network
He initialisation — the scheme this project uses
\[ W^{(\ell)}_{j,i} \;\sim\; \mathcal{N}\!\left(0,\ \frac{2}{n_{\text{in}}}\right) \qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad \texttt{rng.standard\_normal((a,b)) * np.sqrt(2.0 / a)} \]
The variance shrinks as the layer gets wider, keeping the scale of activations roughly constant as signals pass through. The factor of 2 compensates for ReLU discarding half of its input range.
Hidden layer width
Batch size
L2 regularisationthe l2 argument, unused in the shipped run
Stage 11 — inside the trained model

What 101,770 numbers turned into

Before training, the first-layer weights are pure noise from a random number generator. After 30 epochs they are not. Toggle between them.

All 128 first-layer templates
Same 128 tiles, same colour scale. Trained templates show stroke fragments, loops and edges concentrated in the centre where the ink is; the border pixels stay near zero because nothing there was ever informative.

The point of the hidden layer

The hidden layer's job is to move the data somewhere the last layer — which can only draw straight boundaries — is able to separate it. We can see whether it succeeded by projecting both spaces down to 2D with PCA and colouring by the true digit.

Raw pixel space vs. learned feature space 2,500 test digits, PCA to 2D
Stage 12 — evaluation

Where it fails, and how it knows

One accuracy number hides the structure of the errors. The confusion matrix shows exactly which digits get mistaken for which, across all 10,000 test images.

Confusion matrixhover a cell
The mistakes it was most confident about
Click any digit to run it through the network and see the full probability distribution. Several are genuinely ambiguous — the kind of handwriting a person would also hesitate over.

Knowing when to say "I don't know"

The app refuses to answer when it is unsure. The measure it uses is the entropy of the probability distribution: near 0 when one digit dominates, and \(\log 10 \approx 2.303\) when all ten are equally likely.

Shannon entropy of the output distribution
\[ H(\mathbf{p}) \;=\; -\sum_{k=0}^{9} p_k \log p_k \qquad 0 \le H \le \log 10 \approx 2.303 \]
Entropy separates right answers from wrong ones 
src/app.py — the refusal ruleentropy = float(-(p * np.log(np.clip(p, 1e-12, None))).sum())
if entropy > REJECT_ENTROPY:                  # REJECT_ENTROPY = 1.0
    self.digit.config(text='?', fg='#898781')
    self.conf.config(text=f'not confident enough (entropy {entropy:.2f})')
Stage 13 — over to you

Running Sherlock yourself

# 1. train — writes weights.npz
cd src
python3 train.py

# 2. draw digits at it
python3 app.py

Needs Python 3.12+, NumPy and Pillow. Training takes a few minutes on a laptop CPU; there is no GPU code anywhere in the project.

Honest limits

This model recognises MNIST-shaped digits: a single, centred, size-normalised numeral in white on black. It has no concept of multiple digits, rotation, colour, or anything that is not a digit at all — shown a photograph of a cat it will still return one of ten answers, though the entropy check will usually refuse it. The fully-connected architecture is also blind to spatial structure by construction; a convolutional network is the standard next step, and would push test accuracy past 99% on the same data.

Every figure on this page was generated from the code in this repository — training run seed 0, 30 epochs, test accuracy measured once on the 10,000 held-out images. The trained weights are embedded in this page so the live demo runs the same arithmetic in your browser.
